    Chapter 1

    General Introduction

    India extends from 8°4'N to 37°6'N latitude and 68°7'E to 97°25'E longitude, covering 32,87,263 sq. km (2.4% of world land surface, 7th largest). High-yield exam facts include the Tropic of Cancer traversing 8 states, Indian Standard Time (82°30'E) passing near Shankargarh/Prayagraj in UP, and India's 15,106.7 km land borders.

    Geographical Location, Latitudinal Extent & Extreme Pointspp. 7–11

    • India lies entirely in the Northern and Eastern Hemispheres, extending latitudinally from 8°4' N to 37°6' N and longitudinally from 68°7' E to 97°25' E.
    • The mainland of India spans 3,214 km from North to South (Indira Col in Ladakh to Cape Comorin in Kanyakumari) and 2,933 km from West to East (Guhar Moti in Gujarat to Kibithu in Arunachal Pradesh).
    • India covers an area of 32,87,263 sq. km (ISFR: 32,87,469 sq. km), accounting for approximately 2.4% of the world's total land area while sustaining 17.5% of the world's population (Census 2011).
    • India is the seventh-largest country in the world by land area, after Russia, Canada, USA, China, Brazil, and Australia.
    • Indira Point [इंदिरा पॉइंट] (formerly Pygmalion Point or Parsons Point) at 6°45' N latitude on Great Nicobar Island is India's southernmost geographical point; it was partially submerged during the 2004 tsunami.
    • Indira Col in Ladakh marks India's northernmost point; Kibithu in Anjaw district of Arunachal Pradesh marks the easternmost point; and Guhar Moti (Kutch, Gujarat) marks the westernmost point.

    International Land Frontiers, Boundaries & Coastal Borderlandspp. 17–21

    • India shares 15,106.7 km of international land borders with 7 countries: Bangladesh (4,096.7 km - longest), China (3,488 km), Pakistan (3,323 km), Nepal (1,751 km), Myanmar (1,643 km), Bhutan (699 km), and Afghanistan (106 km in PoK - shortest).
    • The international boundary between India and Pakistan is known as the Radcliffe Line [रेडक्लिफ रेखा], drawn in August 1947 by Sir Cyril Radcliffe; Radcliffe line also demarcates the border with Bangladesh.
    • The McMahon Line [मैकमोहन रेखा] was drawn in 1914 at the Simla Convention to demarcate the boundary between British India and Tibet (Arunachal Pradesh sector of India-China border).
    • The Durand Line [डूरंड रेखा] was demarcated in 1893 by Sir Mortimer Durand between British India and Afghanistan; currently it separates Pakistan and Afghanistan, with a 106 km stretch bordering India in Ladakh (PoK).
    • India's total coastline measures 7,516.6 km (mainland coastline: 5,422.6 km, island territories: 2,094 km), touching 9 coastal states: Gujarat (longest coastline ~1,214.7 km), Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Maharashtra, Kerala, Odisha, Karnataka, West Bengal, and Goa.

    Chapter 2

    Physical Division

    India's physical divisions encompass the Northern Himalayan Wall, the Peninsular Plateau (oldest stable Gondwana block), Great Northern Plains, Coastal Plains, and Island Archipelagos. Key exam themes cover Himalayan transverse zones, strategic mountain passes, Peninsular peaks (Anamudi, Doddabetta), and Ten Degree Channel.

    Major Tribes of India, Regional Distribution & Cultural Practicespp. 82–89

    • According to Census 2011, Scheduled Tribes constitute 8.6% of India's total population; Bhils are the largest tribal group in India (over 1.7 crore), followed closely by Gonds and Santhals.
    • Toda tribe [टोडा जनजाति] inhabits the Nilgiri Hills of Tamil Nadu; they are traditional pastoralists centered around sacred water buffalo herds, speak a Dravidian language, and historically practiced fraternal polyandry.
    • Jarawa, Sentinelese, Onge, and Great Andamanese are indigenous hunter-gatherer tribes of Negrito stock inhabiting the Andaman Islands, classified as Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups (PVTGs).
    • Garo, Khasi, and Jaintia tribes of Meghalaya follow a traditional matrilineal descent and matrilocal residence system.
    • Lepcha and Bhutia tribes inhabit Sikkim and the Darjeeling hills of West Bengal; Bodo and Miri tribes are indigenous to Assam; Chenchu tribe inhabits the Nallamala forests of Andhra Pradesh and Telangana.
    • Santhal tribe predominantly inhabits Jharkhand, West Bengal, and Odisha; famous for the historic Santhal Hool (Rebellion) of 1855 led by Sidhu and Kanhu.

    Chapter 5

    Languages of India

    Indian languages belong to four major families: Indo-Aryan (~78%), Dravidian (~20%), Austro-Asiatic (Munda), and Sino-Tibetan. The Eighth Schedule recognizes 22 official languages, with Hindi and Bengali being the most widely spoken, while UP recognizes Hindi and Urdu.

    Linguistic Families of India & Major Language Groupspp. 97–97

    • The Indo-Aryan language family [भारतीय-आर्य भाषा परिवार] is the largest linguistic group in India, spoken by approximately 78% of the population, comprising Hindi, Bengali, Marathi, Gujarati, Punjabi, Sindhi, Odia, Assamese, and Sanskrit.
    • The Dravidian language family [द्रविड़ भाषा परिवार] is the second largest group (~20% speakers), comprising the major literary languages Telugu, Tamil, Kannada, and Malayalam, along with tribal languages like Gondi, Kurukh, and Kui.
    • The Austro-Asiatic (Munda) family [ऑस्ट्रो-एशियाटिक भाषा परिवार] is spoken primarily by indigenous tribes of central and eastern India, including Santhali, Mundari, Ho, Bhumij, and Khasi in Meghalaya.
    • Hindi is the most widely spoken language in India (~43.6% native speakers as per Census 2011), followed by Bengali (8.03%), Marathi (6.86%), Telugu (6.7%), and Tamil (5.7%).
    • According to Ethnologue 2025, Bengali ranks as the 7th most spoken language in the world (~284 million global users) and the second most spoken in the Indian subcontinent after Hindi.

    Scheduled Languages, Classical Status & UP Official Languagespp. 98–98

    • The Eighth Schedule of the Indian Constitution originally listed 14 regional languages in 1950, which has expanded to 22 recognized scheduled languages through three constitutional amendments.
    • Sindhi was added to the Eighth Schedule by the 21st Constitutional Amendment Act (1967); Konkani, Manipuri, and Nepali were added by the 71st Amendment (1992); Bodo, Dogri, Maithili, and Santhali were added by the 92nd Amendment (2003).
    • The Government of India confers Classical Language status [शास्त्रीय भाषा] based on high antiquity of early texts (1500-2000 years); Tamil was declared first in 2004, followed by Sanskrit (2005), Telugu and Kannada (2008), Malayalam (2013), and Odia (2014).
    • In October 2024, five additional languages were granted Classical status: Marathi, Pali, Prakrit, Assamese, and Bengali, bringing the total to 11 Classical Languages.
    • Uttar Pradesh has two officially recognized state languages: Hindi was declared the first official language in 1947, and Urdu was enacted as the second official language through the UP Official Language (Amendment) Act 1989.

    Chapter 6

    Drainage System

    India's drainage systems are divided into perennial Himalayan rivers (Ganga, Indus, Brahmaputra) and rain-fed Peninsular rivers (Godavari, Krishna, Narmada, Kaveri). UPPSC focuses on Ganga's Panch Prayag confluences, rift-valley flowing Narmada-Tapi, and UP rivers (Yamuna, Betwa, Ken, Son, Gomti).

    Chapter 7

    Climate

    India features a tropical monsoon climate governed by the South-West Monsoon (supplying ~75% of annual rainfall) and the winter North-East Monsoon. UPPSC frequently tests Western Disturbances causing winter rains in Western UP and extreme rainfall variations across UP (Gorakhpur highest, Mathura lowest).

    Mechanism of Indian Monsoon & Rainfall Distributionpp. 142–150

    • India's climate is classified as Tropical Monsoon [उष्णकटिबंधीय मानसूनी जलवायु], characterized by seasonal reversal of wind direction driven by differential heating of land and sea and shift of the Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ).
    • दक्षिण-पश्चिम मानसून [South-West Monsoon] (June to September) advances across India in two main branches: the Arabian Sea Branch and the Bay of Bengal Branch, supplying over 75% of India's total annual precipitation.
    • Mawsynram and Cherrapunji on the southern slopes of Khasi Hills in Meghalaya receive the highest average annual rainfall in the world (>1,100 cm) due to the funneling relief of the Meghalaya plateau.
    • The windward western slopes of the Western Ghats receive heavy orographic rainfall exceeding 250 cm, while the leeward Deccan plateau lies in the rain-shadow zone [वृष्टि छाया क्षेत्र] receiving under 60 cm.
    • Global climatic oscillations significantly influence monsoon performance: El Niño generally suppresses Indian monsoon rainfall, whereas La Niña and positive Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) phases promote abundant monsoon rains.

    Western Disturbances, Winter Rainfall & UP Climate Dynamicspp. 151–159

    • पश्चिमी विक्षोभ [Western Disturbances] are extra-tropical temperate cyclonic storms originating over the Mediterranean Sea, steered into northwest India by the subtropical westerly jet stream during winter months (December–February).
    • पश्चिमी विक्षोभ [Western Disturbances] bring light to moderate winter rainfall to Punjab, Haryana, Delhi, and Western Uttar Pradesh, which is immensely beneficial for the रबी [Rabi] wheat crop, while causing heavy snowfall in the Western Himalayas.
    • उत्तर-पूर्वी मानसून / लौटता मानसून [Retreating / उत्तर-पूर्वी मानसून [North-East Monsoon]] (October to December) picks up moisture over the Bay of Bengal and yields heavy winter rainfall along the Coromandel Coast of Tamil Nadu.
    • Within Uttar Pradesh, Gorakhpur district receives the highest annual rainfall (averaging ~184 cm), while Mathura district receives the lowest annual rainfall (averaging ~54 cm).
    • Uttar Pradesh experiences three distinct seasons: Hot Dry Summer (March to June, marked by blistering dusty western winds called 'Loo'), Rainy Season (June to October, driven by the Bay of Bengal monsoon branch entering from the east), and Cold Winter Season (November to February).

    Chapter 8

    Natural Disasters

    India's physiography predisposes it to geological earthquakes (Himalayan Zone V), coastal tropical cyclones (Bay of Bengal), riverine floods (Eastern UP), and arid droughts (Bundelkhand). UPPSC tests seismic classification zones, cyclone naming systems, and disaster management under the NDMA Act 2005.

    Chapter 9

    Soils

    ICAR classifies Indian soils into 8 orders, with Alluvial (~40%), Black / Regur (~15%), Red (~18%), and Laterite being the most significant. UPPSC tests self-ploughing black cotton soils, Gangetic Khadar vs Bangar, sub-Himalayan Bhabhar and Terai, and Bundelkhand soils (Rakar, Parwa, Mar, Kabar).

    Major Soil Groups of India: Alluvial, Black, Red & Lateritepp. 166–172

    • The Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR) classifies Indian soils into 8 major categories, among which जलोढ़ मिट्टी [Alluvial Soil], काली मिट्टी [Black Soil], लाल मिट्टी [Red Soil], and लैटेराइट मिट्टी [Laterite Soil] are commercially paramount.
    • जलोढ़ मिट्टी [Alluvial Soil] is India's most widespread and productive soil group (~40% area), formed by river deposition in the Indo-Gangetic-Brahmaputra plains and coastal deltas; rich in potash and lime, but deficient in nitrogen, phosphorus, and organic humus.
    • काली मिट्टी [Black Soil / रेगुर [Regur]] (काली मिट्टी [Black Cotton Soil]) is derived from the weathering of Deccan basaltic lava (Maharashtra, Gujarat, western MP); dominated by montmorillonite clay, high moisture retention, swells when wet, and develops deep cracks when dry, conferring a 'self-ploughing' [स्वतः जुताई] attribute ideal for dryland cotton cultivation.
    • लाल मिट्टी [Red Soil] develops on crystalline igneous Archean rocks under low rainfall; its red hue is caused by wide diffusion of iron oxides (ferric oxide); highly porous, poor in nitrogen, phosphorus, and humus, requiring irrigation for crops.
    • लैटेराइट मिट्टी [Laterite Soil] forms under high temperatures and alternating intense wet and dry spells through severe leaching [निक्षालन]; rich in iron oxide and aluminium residues, but acidic and poor in lime, silica, and potash; ideal for रोपण फसलें [Plantation Crops] (tea, coffee, rubber, cashew).

    • In Uttar Pradesh, the northern sub-Himalayan belt is divided into: भाबर [Bhabhar] (a narrow gravelly boulder tract where rivers sink underground) and तराई [Terai] (a damp, swampy, silt-rich जलोढ़ [Alluvial] zone south of Bhabhar, highly fertile for sugarcane and paddy).

    Sources of Irrigation in India: Tube-wells, Canals & Tankspp. 188–191

    • Tube-wells and open wells constitute the largest source of irrigation in India (~62%), followed by government and private Canals (~24%), Tanks (~3%), and other sources.
    • Uttar Pradesh ranks #1 in India in net irrigated area and #1 in tubewell-irrigated area, with tube-wells irrigating approximately 80% of the state's net cultivated land.
    • Tanks [तालाब] are the dominant traditional irrigation source in Peninsular South India (Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana) due to the undulating crystalline rocky terrain, which prevents canal excavation and promotes rainwater harvesting in natural depressions.
    • Canal irrigation is most extensively developed in the northern जलोढ़ [Alluvial] plains of Punjab, Haryana, and Uttar Pradesh due to perennial snow-fed rivers and soft, easily excavated alluvial soils.
    • Micro-irrigation techniques (Drip and Sprinkler irrigation under Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchayee Yojana - PMKSY) are heavily promoted for water-use efficiency in water-stressed arid regions.

    Canal Systems of Uttar Pradesh & Inter-Basin River Linkspp. 192–195

    • शारदा नहर [Sharda Canal] is the longest and most extensive canal network in Uttar Pradesh (completed in 1928), originating from the Banbasa Barrage on the Sharda River (Kali river) on the India-Nepal border.
    • ऊपरी गंगा नहर [Upper Ganga Canal] was engineered by Sir Proby Cautley and inaugurated in 1854; it originates from Bhimoda Barrage near Haridwar, irrigating the western Doab region of UP.
    • निचली गंगा नहर [Lower Ganga Canal] was constructed in 1878, originating from the Narora Barrage on the Ganga in Bulandshahr district, irrigating central UP plains.

    • Betwa Canal originates from the Parichha Barrage on the Betwa river in Jhansi district, providing vital irrigation to the drought-prone Bundelkhand districts of Jhansi, Jalaun, and Hamirpur.
    • The landmark Ken-Betwa Link Project [केन-बेतवा नदी जोड़ो परियोजना] is India's first national river interlinking project under the National Perspective Plan, building the Daudhan Dam to transfer surplus water from Ken river (MP) to Betwa basin (UP), irrigating over 2.5 lakh hectares in Bundelkhand.

    Iconic Multipurpose River Valley Projects of Indiapp. 195–204

    • Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru hailed multi-purpose river valley projects as the 'Temples of Modern India' [आधुनिक भारत के मंदिर] for their foundational role in industrial and agricultural self-reliance.
    • Damodar Valley Corporation [दामोदर घाटी निगम] (DVC), established in July 1948, was independent India's first multipurpose river valley project, modeled directly after the Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA) of the USA; major dams include Tilaiya, Maithon, and Panchet.
    • Bhakra-Nangal Project on the Satluj River is a joint venture of Punjab, Haryana, and Rajasthan; Bhakra Dam is one of the highest concrete straight gravity dams in the world (226 m), creating the Gobind Sagar reservoir in Himachal Pradesh.
    • Tehri Dam [टिहरी बांध] on the Bhagirathi River (at confluence with Bhilangana) in Tehri Garhwal (Uttarakhand) is the highest earth-and-rockfill dam in India (260.5 m height).
    • Hirakud Dam [हीराकुंड बांध] on the Mahanadi River in Sambalpur district of Odisha is the longest earthen dam in the world (~25.8 km total length with dykes).
    • Sardar Sarovar Dam on the Narmada River in Navagam, Gujarat, is a massive concrete gravity dam serving Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, and Rajasthan; opposed by the Narmada Bachao Andolan led by Medha Patkar.

    Genesis, Inputs & High Yielding Varieties of Green Revolutionpp. 224–226

    • हरित क्रांति [Green Revolution] in India was launched in 1966-67 (during the Annual Plans period) to overcome severe food deficits and end reliance on US PL-480 food imports.
    • Dr. Norman Ernest Borlaug (USA/CIMMYT Mexico) is recognized as the 'Father of the हरित क्रांति [Green Revolution] in the World'; he received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1970 for breeding high-yielding semi-dwarf wheat varieties using Norin-10 dwarfing genes.
    • Dr. M.S. Swaminathan [डॉ. एम.एस. स्वामीनाथन] is revered as the 'Father of the हरित क्रांति [Green Revolution] in India', spearheading the adaptation and field deployment of Mexican semi-dwarf varieties (Lerma Rojo 64A and Sonora 64).
    • Govind Ballabh Pant University of Agriculture & Technology (Pantnagar, established in 1960 in erstwhile UP, now Uttarakhand) served as the pioneering cradle of the हरित क्रांति [Green Revolution] in India.
    • The technological package of the हरित क्रांति [Green Revolution] relied on the synergistic 'seed-fertilizer-water technology': High-Yielding Variety (HYV) seeds, assured tubewell/canal irrigation, chemical fertilizers (ideal NPK ratio 4:2:1), and plant protection pesticides.

    Major Pulses: Gram, Tur/Arhar & Nitrogen Fixation Traitspp. 250–251

    • दलहन [Pulses] constitute the primary dietary source of protein for India's predominantly vegetarian population; leguminous pulse crops harbor symbiotic Rhizobium bacteria in root nodules that fix atmospheric nitrogen, restoring soil fertility (except Arhar which has low fixation).
    • India is simultaneously the world's largest producer, largest consumer, and largest importer of दलहन [Pulses].
    • Gram [चना] (Chickpea) is the single most important pulse crop in India, accounting for nearly 40-45% of total pulse production; a रबी [Rabi] crop cultivated on light loamy and clayey soils; prominent varieties include 'Radhey', 'Pusa-256' (KBG-38), and 'Avarodhi' (wilt-resistant).
    • Arhar / Tur [अरहर/तूर] (Pigeonpea) is the second most important pulse crop, cultivated as a deep-rooted खरीफ [Kharif] crop with a long maturity period (6-9 months); leading producers are Maharashtra and Madhya Pradesh; popular varieties include 'Bahar', 'UPAS-120', and 'Malviya Chamatkar'.
    • Moong (Green gram) and Urad (Black gram) are short-duration दलहन [Pulses] cultivated in both खरीफ [Kharif] and जायद [Zaid] seasons, fitting well into crop rotations.

    Four Varieties of Commercial Silk & Sericulture in Indiapp. 253–253

    • रेशम कीट पालन [Sericulture] is the agro-based practice of rearing silkworms for the production of raw रेशम [Silk]; India is the second largest producer of silk in the world after China.
    • India possesses the unique global distinction of commercially producing all four known varieties of natural रेशम [Silk]: शहतूती [Mulberry Silk], तसर [Tasar Silk], एरी [Eri Silk], and मूगा [Muga Silk].

    • Varanasi (Kashi) in Uttar Pradesh is globally renowned for its traditional handloom Banarasi रेशम [Silk] Sarees [बनारसी रेशमी साड़ी] featuring intricate gold and silver zari brocade work (GI tagged).

    Tea & Coffee: Ecological Requirements & Producing Regionspp. 254–257

    • रोपण फसलें [Plantation Crops] are capital-intensive commercial crops cultivated on large estates for domestic consumption and export.
    • Tea [चाय] (Camellia sinensis) is a shade-loving sub-tropical beverage crop requiring 20°-30°C temperature, heavy rainfall (150-250 cm) well-distributed throughout the year, and deep, friable, well-drained acidic loamy soils on gentle hill slopes (stagnant water rots roots).
    • Assam is the leading producer of tea in India, accounting for over 50% of national output (Brahmaputra and Surma valleys), followed by West Bengal (Dooars and Darjeeling); Darjeeling Tea was awarded India's first Geographical Indication (GI) tag in 2004-05.
    • Coffee [कॉफी] requires warm and humid climate (15°-28°C), 150-200 cm rainfall, and fertile humus-rich soils on hill slopes sheltered from direct blazing sunlight.
    • Karnataka is the undisputed leader in coffee production, contributing roughly 70% of India's coffee, centered in the Western Ghats districts of Kodagu, Chikmagalur, and Hassan.
    • Two commercial coffee species are grown in India: Coffea arabica (superior mild aroma, sensitive to rust) and Coffea robusta (hardy, higher yield, used in instant coffee); Coffee Board is headquartered at Bengaluru.

    Jhuming Agriculture

    Shifting cultivation (slash-and-burn / Jhuming) is practiced by tribal communities across hilly forest tracts, causing severe soil erosion and forest loss. UPPSC tests the distinctive local vernacular names of shifting cultivation across different Indian states.

    Shifting Cultivation: Agronomic Practices & Ecological Effectspp. 262–262

    • झूम कृषि [Shifting Cultivation] (Slash-and-Burn agriculture / कर्तन एवं दहन प्रणाली) is a primitive subsistence farming system where a patch of forest is cleared by felling and burning vegetation, cultivated for 2-3 years, and then abandoned to fallow for natural regeneration.
    • Ash from burnt trees adds potash to the soil temporarily, but the rapid decline in natural soil fertility and weed infestation forces tribes to shift to a fresh forest plot.
    • Shortening of the fallow cycle (from 15-20 years historically to 2-4 years currently) due to population pressure has caused catastrophic deforestation, accelerated soil erosion, and biodiversity loss.
    • झूम कृषि [Shifting Cultivation] is most prevalent among indigenous tribal communities inhabiting the hill tracts of Northeast India (Assam, Meghalaya, Nagaland, Mizoram, Manipur, and Arunachal Pradesh).
    • According to 2024-25 data, farming of cloves is done in Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Karnataka. Hence the question asked is wrong. UPPSC
    • According to 2024-25 data, the three leading cashew nut producers in India are – Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh and Odisha. UPPSC
    • When the question was asked option (a) was correct answer. Currently, its answer would be Odisha and Madhya Pradesh. UPPSC

    Regional Local Nomenclature of Shifting Cultivation Across Statespp. 263–264

    • झूम कृषि [Shifting Cultivation] is identified by specific local vernacular names across different Indian states and hill regions, a topic tested with high frequency in UPPSC exams:
    • Jhum [झूम]: North-Eastern states (Assam, Meghalaya, Nagaland, Mizoram, Arunachal Pradesh).
    • Bewar [बेवर] or Dahiya [दहिया]: Madhya Pradesh (practiced traditionally by Baiga and Gond tribes).
    • Podu [पोडू], Dabi [दाबी], Koman [कोमान], or Bringa [बृंगा]: Odisha and Andhra Pradesh.
    • Kumari [कुमारी]: Western Ghats hill tracts in Kerala and Karnataka.
    • Valre [वालरे] or Waltre [वाल्टरे]: South-eastern Rajasthan (practiced by Bhils).
    • Khil [खिल]: Himalayan belt of Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand.
    • Kuruwa [कुरुवा]: Santhal Pargana and Chota Nagpur plateau in Jharkhand.
    • Penda [पेंडा]: Bastar district of Chhattisgarh.

    Mineral Resources

    India's mineral wealth is concentrated in Pre-Cambrian Dharwar rocks (metallic ores) and Gondwana sedimentary basins (coal). UPPSC questions focus on coal basins (Jharia, Raniganj, Singrauli), iron ore (Bailadila, Kudremukh), copper (Malanjkhand, Khetri), and UP minerals in Sonbhadra, Banda, and Prayagraj.

    Geological Formations & Major Coalfields of Indiapp. 285–295

    • Gondwana rock formations [गोंडवाना शैल] contain approximately 98% of India's total कोयला [Coal] reserves and over 99% of its annual coal production; primarily bituminous, non-coking coal.
    • Damodar Valley coalfield is the primary repository of metallurgical coking कोयला [Coal] in India; Jharia in Dhanbad district of Jharkhand is India's richest coalfield.
    • Raniganj in West Bengal is the oldest commercial कोयला [Coal] mine in India, where coal mining commenced in 1774 during the East India Company era.
    • Singrauli coalfield spans Sonbhadra district of Uttar Pradesh and Singrauli district of MP, supplying कोयला [Coal] to mega ताप विद्युत [Thermal Power] plants of NTPC.
    • Talcher in the Mahanadi valley (Odisha) and Singareni in the Godavari valley (Telangana) are major non-coking coalfields.
    • Neyveli in Cuddalore district of Tamil Nadu possesses the largest deposits of Lignite [लिग्नाइट] (brown कोयला [Coal]) in India, operated by NLC India Ltd.
    • Dharwar system is the most important mineralized rock system in India. These rocks are economically very important as they possess valuable minerals like high-grade iron-ore, manganese, copper, lead, gold, etc. UPPSC ×2

    Petroleum, Natural Gas Fields, Offshore Basins & Mathura Refinerypp. 323–329

    • Crude oil was first discovered in India at Makum (Assam) in 1867; Digboi [डिगबोई] in Tinsukia district of Assam is the oldest operating oilfield and oil refinery in India, commissioned in 1901.
    • Mumbai High [बॉम्बे हाई] (discovered in 1974 by ONGC using the jack-up rig 'Sagar Samrat') is India's largest domestic offshore crude oil producing field in the Arabian Sea.
    • Ankleshwar in Bharuch district of Gujarat is a major onshore oilfield, once termed the 'Fountain of Prosperity' by Jawaharlal Nehru; Kalol, Mehsana, and Nawagam are other Gujarat fields.
    • Krishna-Godavari (KG-D6) Basin in the Bay of Bengal holds vast deepwater natural gas reserves; Barmer basin in Rajasthan (Mangala, Bhagyam, Aishwarya) produces substantial onshore crude.
    • Jamnagar Refinery (Reliance Industries in Gujarat) is the world's largest grassroots petroleum refining complex.
    • Mathura Oil Refinery [मथुरा तेल शोधनागार] (IOCL) in Uttar Pradesh was commissioned in 1982, processing crude transported via pipeline from Salaya (Gujarat); environmental emissions led to Supreme Court directives to protect the Taj Mahal from acid rain.

    Tourism

    Incredible India Circuits, UNESCO World Heritage Sites & Pilgrimagepp. 407–409

    • Strategic maritime channels tested by UPPSC: Ten Degree Channel [10° चैनल] (10° N latitude) separates Andaman Islands from Nicobar Islands; Nine Degree Channel [9° चैनल] separates Minicoy Island from the main Lakshadweep archipelago; Eight Degree Channel [8° चैनल] separates Minicoy (India) from Maldives.

    Universe Origin, Big Bang & Stellar Lifecycles

    • The first rational perspective regarding the origin of the planets was probably proposed by a French naturalist ‘Comte de Buffon’ in 1749. According to the number of stars participating in the origin of planets, the scientific concepts have been divided into two parts- (1) Monistic concept and (2) Dualistic concept.
    • The latest theory regarding the origin of the universe is the महाविस्फोट सिद्धांत [Big Bang Theory] Theory.
    • After the explosion, the universe expanded in all directions and different galaxies of different shapes were formed. Thus, the universe comprises of an infinite number of galaxies. It is estimated that there are appx. 100-200 billion galaxies in the universe and every galaxy is estimated to have around 100 billion stars. Our galaxy is known as an Akash Ganga or मंदाकिनी [Milky Way Galaxy].
    • In 2005, the Spitzer Space Telescope gave clear evidences that our galaxy (the मंदाकिनी [Milky Way Galaxy]) is barred spiral in shape, hence disapproving the earlier theories.
    • The formation of the star passes through different phases. In the first phase, a proto-star is formed after that the star enters the second phase i.e., the main sequence Star. A star of the size of our sun stays in this phase for around 9 or 10 billion years. After this phase, the fuel of the star i.e., hydrogen starts getting used up to an extent that the star enters the third phase i.e., towards its death.
    • In this phase, the outer layer of the star expands greatly, It becomes a Red Giant or Red Supergiant.

    The Solar System, Sun & Planetary Dynamics

    • Under the Monistic concept, Immanuel Kant’s Gaseous Hypothesis and Pierre-Simon Laplace’s Nebular Hypothesis became famous. Under the Dualistic concept, Chamberlin and Moulton Planetesimal Hypothesis, James Jeans and Jefferys Tidal Hypothesis, H.N. Russell and Lyttleton Binary Star Hypothesis etc. became noteworthy.
    • Georges Lemaitre (1894-1966) was the first to present the idea of an expanding universe. Later in 1967, Robert Wagoner presented the interpretation of this theory. The महाविस्फोट सिद्धांत [Big Bang Theory] theory explains how 13.7 or 13.8 billion years ago universe expanded from a very high density and high-temperature state.
    • The shape of the Galaxies varies in shape and size. Some are spiral, some are irregular and some are elliptical.
    • The universe is a collection of infinite galaxies. Every galaxy has around 100 billion stars. These stars are formed as a result of the presence of hydrogen and helium gases in their unified form (Nebulae). The gravitational force keeps the gases and dust particles in the unified form. Velocity, high temperature and organizational processes are the factors behind the formation of a star.
    • The lifespan of any star depends upon its size. A star of the size of our sun (one solar mass) has a lifespan of around 9 or 10 billion years. The bigger the star is, the shorter is its life span. For example, a star whose surface temperature is more than 30000 Kelvin and which is 100 times the size of our sun has a life span of only a few million years. After the main sequence life of the star ends, it enters in the elderly phase.
    • After the red Giant phase, a star witnesses an explosion in the form of a Nova or Supernova, thus entering its last stage of life. Depending upon its size it can end up in- a Black Dwarf, Neutron star or a कृष्ण विवर [Black Hole]. Sun like small stars – after the Red Giant phase and Nova explosion if the stellar mass is less than 1.44 solar Masses, the star will end up being a White Dwarf first and then into a Black Dwarf. Medium sized stars - after the Red Giant Phase and Supernova explosion, if the stellar mass is between 1.44 to 3 solar masses, then a star can convert into a Neutron Star (Pulsar). Large size stars – those which have a stellar mass more than 3 times that of our sun. These stars have the possibility to convert into a black hole after a supernova explosion.

(Pr e) 2024 Ans. (a) Chemical weathering is the process that breaks down rock through chemical changes. Rainfall and temperature can affect the rate at which rocks weather. High temperatures and greater rainfall increase the rate of chemical weathering. Rocks in tropical regions exposed to abundant rainfall and hot temperatures weather much faster than similar rocks residing in cold, dry regions. Rainwater may contain impurities from the atmosphere in the form of dust particles and dissolved gases like oxygen, nitrogen and carbon dioxide. When water (e.g. rainwater) mixes with carbon dioxide gas in the air or in air pockets in soil, a weak acid solution, called carbonic acid, is produced. When carbonic acid flows through the cracks of some rocks, it chemically reacts with the rock causing some of it to dissolve. This process is called carbonation. It is very active in limestone regions. Rainwater contains dissolved oxygen from the atmosphere, which can participate in oxidation processes that contribute to weathering. Oxygen in rainwater reacts with minerals, particularly iron-bearing ones, to form oxides or rust, leading to weakening and breakdown. Hence, both Statement-II and Statement-III are correct and both of them explain Statement-I. The ज्वालामुखी [Volcano]

    • ज्वार-भाटा [Tides] are the rise and fall of sea levels caused by the combined effects of the gravitational forces exerted by the Moon and the Sun, and the rotation of the Earth. The rotation of the Earth creates two forces - the centripetal and centrifugal forces, which play a major role in the formation of tides. This means that the side of the Earth that faces the Moon experiences a gravitational force, greater than that of the Earth itself. Hence we experience high tides. On the other hand the side of Earth that is facing away from moon experiences less gravitational force from the Moon, as a result, we experience high (indirect high tides) tides. Between these two high tides water level goes down this is called low tides (ebb). Thus in the time span of 24 hrs. and 50 minutes (or 52 minutes) we experience two High Tides and two Low Tides.     Atmospheric Composition, Trace Gases & Greenhouse Effect

    • The atmosphere is composed of various gases, of which 99% is made up of nitrogen and oxygen. Other 1% comprises argon, carbon dioxide, neon, krypton, helium, Hydrogen, and xenon. Gas Formula Presence in वायुमंडल [Atmosphere] (in percentage) Nitrogen N 2 78.084 Oxygen O 2 20.947 Argon Ar 0.934 Carbon dioxide CO2 0.0426 Neon Ne 0.0018 Helium He 0.0005 Krypton Kr 0.0001 Hydrogen H 2 0.000053 Xenon Xe 0.000009 ∗Heavy gases in the atmosphere descend whereas lighter gases are found in the upper layers as they ascend. As a result CO2 gases extend up to 20 km from the surface, oxygen, and nitrogen up to 100 km, hydrogen up to 125 km and other gases rise far above 125 km except ozone. The atmosphere is made up of different layers of gases with varying densities and temperatures. Based on these factors different layers of the atmosphere are as follows- (1) क्षोभमंडल [Troposphere] – The lowest layer of the atmosphere is called troposphere. All weather activities like clouds, hail, fog, blizzards, thunder, windstorms, etc. are confined to the troposphere. The most important characteristic of the troposphere is that there is a decrease of 6.5 o C with an increase of every 1000 m in altitude. This decrease in temperature with an increase in altitude is known as normal lapse rate. The upper boundary of the troposphere is called tropopause. (2) समतापमंडल [Stratosphere] – Stratosphere (15-50 km) is the second most important layer of the atmosphere. It lies between mesosphere (above) and troposphere (below). This layer of atmosphere is very dry in nature and has the least amount of water vapor in it. As a result, there is no weather activity in stratosphere. The stratosphere is used for aviation purposes as the absence of weather activities makes this layer ideal for flying. Ozone layer is found in this sphere. (3) मध्यमंडल [Mesosphere] – This layer is found at an altitude of 50 to 80 km. The upper ceiling of mesosphere is called mesopause. (4) आयनमंडल [Ionosphere] – It is an electrically conducting layer, that makes radio wave transmission possible over long distances. Ionosphere extends from 80 to 640 km.

    The Atmospheric Pressure

    Examines atmospheric pressure distribution, barometer measurements, and permanent planetary pressure belts. Highlights the Equatorial Low (Doldrums), Subtropical Highs (Horse Latitudes), and Sub-polar Lows.

    UPPSC asks most here

    1. Humidity is the amount of water vapour in the air. In summer, humidity is very high therefore weather is muggy. Absolute humidi...UDA/LDA Pre ’021 paper

    Atmospheric Pressure Principles, Measurement & Isobars

    • Atmospheric pressure is measured using a barometer. It is measured, as the force exerted per unit area of the barometer. A sudden fall in the level of barometer is a sign of an upcoming storm. If the readings of a barometer fall and then start rising slowly it denotes that there will be rainfall.
    • The horizontal distribution of atmospheric pressure is shown by using isobars.
    • आर्द्रता [Humidity] is the amount of water vapour in the air. In summer, humidity is very high therefore weather is muggy. Absolute humidity is the weight of water vapour per unit volume, usually expressed in grains per cubic foot. UPPSC

    Global Pressure Belts: Doldrums & Horse Latitudes

    • A continuous rise in the level of mercury in the barometer is a sign of an anticyclone and clear weather.
    • An isobar is an imaginary line that connects points having same atmospheric pressure at mean sea level. ∗Based on the process of origin, pressure belts can be divided into two parts- (1) Based on thermogenesis – pressure belts thus formed are equatorial low-pressure belts and polar high-pressure belts. (2) Based on motion-pressure belts thus formed are sub- tropical high-pressure belts and sub-polar low-pressure belts. ∗Equatorial Low-Pressure Belts – The belt extends between 5o north and south of Equator. The equator receives vertical rays of the sun throughout the year. As a result, the air gets heated and starts rising up. Hence the region always experiences low pressure. The surface air of the region moves with very slow velocity as a result of which the environment here is quite calm. This is the reason this pressure belt is also called शांत कटिबंध / डोलड्रम्स [Doldrums]. • Sub-tropical High-Pressure Belt – the belt is found between 30o-35o latitudes in both hemispheres. The air rising from the equator starts becoming cooler in the upper layers of atmosphere and hence begins sinking near 30o-35o latitudes. Simultaneously the air from the sub-polar low-pressure belts also starts descending in this region due to Earth's rotation thus a high-pressure zone is created which gives birth to sub- tropical high pressure belt. The pressure belt is highly mobile in nature, thus it is also called Horse अक्षांश [Latitude]. • Sub-Polar Low-Pressure Belt – This pressure belt is found between 60o-65o latitudes in both hemispheres. Though the temperature in this region is low throughout the year the region experiences low pressure. This is due to the fact that rotation of the Earth causes the air to spread and displaces it. As a result low pressure is created. • Polar High-Pressure Belts – The poles and the regions in close proximity to them experience high pressure because the region is very cold which causes the air to become heavy and start descending creating high pressure.

The continuity of sub-polar low pressure belt disrupted in the Northern Hemisphere due to large landmass along 600N latitude while in Southern hemisphere this low pressure belt is more pronounced and stable due to the vast ocean presence and lack of landmass. 2. Wh ich of the following latitudes (north or south) would you associate with 'Horse अक्षांश [Latitudes]' ? (a) 30° (b) 45° (c) 60° (d) 23 21 0 U.P. Lower (Spl) (Pre) 2008 Ans. (a) The horse latitudes are located at about 30° to 35° north and south of the Equator. In the northern hemisphere it is called the north subtropical high-pressure belt and in the southern hemisphere, it is known as the south subtropical high-pressure belt. The existence of these pressure belts is due to the fact that the rising air of the equatorial region is deflected towards poles due to the earth’s rotation. After becoming cold and heavy, it descends in these regions due to Earth rotation and gets piled up. This results in high pressure. Calm conditions with feeble and variable winds are found here. In ancient times vessels with a cargo of horses passing through these belts found difficulty in sailing under these calm conditions. They used to throw a few horses in to the sea in order to make the vessels lighter. Thus, these belts or latitudes came to be known as ‘horse latitudes’. 3. Consider the following statements:

    Forces Governing Winds: Coriolis Effect & Ferrel's Law

    • The movement of air as a result of the difference in horizontal air pressure is known as wind. Wind in general flows from a high- pressure area to a low-pressure area. If the earth were still and flat, the winds would blow from a high-pressure area directly to a low-pressure area along the isobaric lines at an angle of 90o. However, the Earth is geoid in shape and rotates on its own axis. Hence winds under the influence of dynamic forces keep shifting their trajectory. Types of Winds – There are basically three types of wind- Planetary Winds – Winds blowing constantly in a particular direction throughout the year are called planetary winds. The main planetary winds are – trade winds, westerlies and polar easterlies.
    • पछुआ पवनें [Westerlies]- They blow from sub-tropical high-pressure belts (30o-35o) toward sub-polar low-pressure belts (60 o-65o) in both the hemisphere. Since there is more landmass in Northern Hemisphere compared to Southern Hemisphere the westerlies in the former case are more complex, and they are less influential in summers as compared to winter.
    • Wellington (New Zealand) is the only capital in the world that lies in the path of Roaring Forties.
    • Land and Sea Breezes only cover 20 to 30 km of the area including the coastal area. During daytime the land heats up faster than the nearby sea as a result low pressure is created over land and thus cool and moist winds blow from sea to land. This wind is called a sea breeze . There is a complete reversal in the direction of the wind during the night. As a result, winds blow from land to sea. This wind is called Land breeze. • Mountain and घाटी [Valley] Breeze - During daytime the air heats up and rises along the slope of the mountain. This is known as Valley Breeze (Anabatic flow). During the night the air gets cooler and heavier as a result it starts descending along the slope of the mountain. This is known as Mountain Breeze (Katabatic flow). (3) स्थानीय पवनें [Local Winds: चिनूक पवन [Chinook: Snow Eater], फ़ॉन पवन [Foehn: Warm dry alpine wind], सिरोको पवन [Sirocco: Blood rain wind], मिस्ट्रल पवन [Mistral: Cold Rhone wind], Khamsin] – These winds are generated as a result of regional differences in temperature or air pressure. Hence, they affect a very small area. ∗The Mediterranean Sea is located between 30o to 40o North अक्षांश [Latitudes]. Hence, the sea comes under the influence of the sub-tropical high-pressure belt. This belt is mobile in nature. During summers, the trade winds blow in these latitudes and in winter these latitudes come under the influence of westerlies. This means that the westerlies blow towards North east from this region and व्यापारिक पवनें [Trade Winds] blow towards south west from this region.

    Global Planetary Winds: Trade Winds, Westerlies & Roaring Forties

    • Trade winds are winds blowing from sub- tropical high-pressure belts toward equatorial low-pressure belts in both the hemispheres.
    • Due to the presence of less landmass in the Southern Hemisphere the westerlies travel at such a high speed causes them to become stormy. It is because of this high intensity of the westerlies in the southern hemisphere that around 40o latitudes they are known as Roaring Forties, around 50o latitude they are called Furious Fifties and around 60o latitude they are called Shrieking Sixties.
    • Polar winds blow from polar high-pressure belt to sub-polar low-pressure belt. Periodic winds – Winds are those that reverse their direction as per season or time. The important periodic winds are – monsoonal winds, land and sea breezes, breezes of mountains and valleys. Monsoonal winds are those that completely reverse their direction according to seasons. During the six months of summer they blow from sea to land and during the six month of winter they blow from land to sea.
    • The Coriolis force causes winds to deflect to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern Hemisphere (Ferrel's Law). UPPSC

Australia 133562 3 8 Indonesia 95969 2 9 India 72739 2 10 Peru 67160 2 Top 10 Countries for annual net gain in forest area, 2015-2025 Forest Area Ranking Country 1000 ha/yr Percentage 1 China 1686 0.77 2 Russian Federation 942 0.11 3 India 191 0.27 4 Turkiye 118 0.53 5 Australia 105 0.08 6 France 95.9 0.56 7 Indonesia 94.1 0.10 8 South Africa 87.6 0.39 9 Canada 82.5 0.02 10 Vietnam 72.8 0.51 • Tropical Evergreen Forests – They are found on both the sides of the equator between 10 oN and 10oS latitudes. The equatorial region remains hot throughout the year and as a result, there is a lot of rainfall throughout the year. Hence, the equatorial region is covered with evergreen forests. These forests are found in abundance in three diverse regions of the world – (1) Amazon Basin – The region includes Brazil, Bolivia, Peru, Ecuador, Colombia, Venezuela, Guyana and Suriname. (2) Congo Basin – The region includes the Republic of Congo, Cameroon, Central African Republic, Gabon, Equatorial Guinea and Democratic Republic of Congo. (3) Borneo- Mekong - Southeast Asia Basin - The region is composed of two sub-regions, the द्वीप [Island] of Borneo and the Mekong River.
    • Maximum plant species are found in the evergreen rainforests. Hardwood trees like – Rosewood, Aabnoos, Mahogany etc. are found in these forests. • Tropical पर्णपाती वन [Deciduous Forest] – They are also known as monsoonal forests. They are mostly found in India, northern Australia, Indonesia the Central America. There are two distinctive seasons (moist and dry) in these forests. India and its nearby regions experience three distinctive seasons thus even the forests of the area experience seasonal changes. The main flora of these forests includes Sal, Teak, Neem and Rosewood. Apart from these other trees, herbs and shrubs are also found. • Temperate Evergreen Forests – They are found in the coastal areas of mid-latitudes. They are normally found on the eastern sides of the continent such as south east USA, South China and southeastern Brazil. Temperate evergreen forests are dominated by specific species of trees. The trees have broad leaves and hardwood for example – Oak, Laurel, Magnolia, and Eucalyptus etc. • Mediterranean Forest – These forests are found in the mid-latitudes on the western and southwestern parts of the continent. They are located in regions receiving winter rainfall. Mediterranean forests are mostly found in the regions of Africa, Europe and Asia that lie in proximity to the Mediterranean Sea. These forests are also found in California and southwestern Australia. The main trees of the region are Cork, Oak, Olives, Plums, Chestnut, Pine etc. The Mediterranean region is famous for the production of Citrus fruits such as Grapes, Lemons, Oranges, Olives, Pears, Pomegranate, etc. •Temperate Coniferous Forests – Also known as टैगा वन [Taiga / Boreal Forest] Forest. They are found between 50 o to 60o North latitude. To their north they have tundra and to their south, they have deciduous forests. They are found in regions of North America, Eurasia and sub-polar regions. They are found in Canada, Europe, Asia and the USA. Temperate coniferous forests cover the largest area in the world. (b) German-Russian botanist and climatologist Vladimir Koppen presented a descriptive classification of the world's climate in the year 1884, which was revised and refined in the years 1918, 1931 and 1936. Koppen has considered vegetation as the true indicator of climate. This has made the five vegetation zones of the world proposed by Candoll in 1874 AD the basis of the division of the world's climate. Later, like Koppen, Thornthwaite also propounded that vegetation is an indicator of climate and that the amount of rainfall and temperature has a substantial effect on vegetation, but he took evaporation into account. On this basis, Thornthwaite has given importance to precipitation effectiveness in demarcation of climate. Thornthwaite has accepted vegetation as an indirect element of climate. 46.     Cartographic Principles, Map Projections & Scales

    • Maps provide us with relevant information regarding regional, territorial and local changes.
    • Contours represent elevation topography in comparison to the sea level. It is the most practical and widely used method in showing elevations on a map. When the contours of Isotypes are drawn very close to each other then it signifies steep slopes. Isohypse - isohypse or height contour is a line of equal geopotential height, which are shown on a constant pressure surface. Isogonic lines show the earth’s magnetic declination on a map. Isobaths are imaginary lines, a map that links points at the same depth below the water surface.
    • Isohyets are lines on the map joining areas having an equal amount of rainfall.
    • Isohalines are lines on the map joining areas having an equal amount of salinity.
    • An imaginary line or a line on a map joining points on the Earth’s surface at which the magnetic declination is the same called, isogonal. UPPSC

    Isopleth Isolines & Contours (Isobars, Isotherms, Isohyets, Isohalines)

    • Isopleth maps provide us information about regions or areas having continuous distribution. Thus isopleths are lines joining places of equal value of quantity, intensity, equal pressure, equal temperature, equal rainfall, equal salinity etc. A very relevant and precise data is required for drawing the lines of isopleths. If there is equitable distribution of the given subject then isopleths become very useful. Moreover, the use of isopleths becomes difficult if the subject is in constant fluctuation for exp. population density.
    • Isobars are imaginary lines drawn on the maps that links areas having equal air pressure at mean sea level.
    • Isonifs are lines on the map joining areas having an equal amount of snowfall.
    • Ferdinand Magellan was a Portuguese explorer and the first person to circumnavigate the world.
    • Isopleths are contour lines connecting geographical locations having equal numerical values of a variable (temperature, pressure, rain). UPPSC
    • Isobars connect points of equal atmospheric pressure, while Isotherms connect points experiencing equal mean temperatures. UPPSC
    • Isohyets are isolines connecting places receiving equal amounts of rainfall during a specified duration. UPPSC
    • Isohalines connect points of equal salinity in oceans and enclosed seas, indicating salinity gradients. UPPSC
    • समोच्च रेखाएं [Contour Lines] connect points of equal elevation above sea level; closely spaced contours indicate steep topography. UPPSC
